newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: N.Z. dollar dives triggering interest rate jump.
newsitem.headline: N.Z. dollar dives triggering interest rate jump.

text.p: The New Zealand dollar on Friday plummeted more than one U.S. cent from its Thursday close to under 65 cents, its lowest level since December 1996.
Dealers said the kiwi was being pummelled by hedge funds and had almost no defences.
"The prospects are gloomy. There are no buyers on the horizon whatsoever," one said.
"Kiwi is in free-fall," said another. "All the longs are getting out and I wouldn't be surprised if we saw 0.6450 today."
By 11.00 a.m. (2300 GMT) the currency was at 0.6488/95 to the U.S. unit and all talk was of the possibility of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (central bank) taking some sort of action.
Unlike other central banks, New Zealand's RBNZ has no key interest rate mechanism with which it can try to steer short term monetary conditions.
It relies instead on a formula called the Monetary Conditions Index (MCI), that brings together the New Zealand dollar and the market-traded 90-day bank bill rate.
In recent weeks the market has responded to a phase of downward pressure on the kiwi dollar by raising short-dated bill rates to keep the RBNZ's desired balance on the MCI.
In morning trade, the bill rate surged to compensate for the dollar's slide to stand at 8.48 percent, up nearly 80 basis points from Thursday's close of 7.70 percent.
This level of short-term money market interest rate clearly threatens to knock-on to mortgage rates, bankers say.
New Zealand variable home loan rates currently cluster around 8.95 percent with some as low as 8.20 percent.
On Thursday afternoon one large home lender, Countrywide Bank, said it would be obliged to raise its variable mortgage unless there was an imminent reversal in short bill rates.

Like others in the market, Countrywide criticised policy makers for setting the preconditions which were now placing upward pressure on rates at a time when the economy is in a low growth phase and showing extremely low inflation trends.
The RBNZ could be forced to use one of its few remaining policy levers, its overnight cash target, as a last-ditch mechanism to achieve a tightening to counter the lower dollar.
However, some analysts believe the currency will soon find a base and a brief, sharp tightening in bill rates would be followed by a return of conditions to their previous levels.
Michael Workman, currency strategist with Commonwealth Bank of Australia, told Reuters Financial Television that the kiwi dollar was presently a one-way bet.
"Over the next week or so we believe the downside of the New Zealand dollar will continue to dominate the outlook.
"We are looking for it to go down towards the 64 cent level against the (U.S.) dollar in the very short term," he said.
He argued that if the market's adjustment in bill rates was sufficient the RBNZ would not have to intervene by seeking tighter monetary conditions.

During this week there has been a growing awareness in the New Zealand market that some international traders are looking at the kiwi dollar in the same light as the South-East Asian currencies which have been attacked in recent weeks.
The Australian Financial Review said on Friday the kiwi appeared to have emerged as a new target for the powerful hedge funds, often U.S.-based.
It quoted John Noonan, head of international sales for National Australia Bank in Singapore, as saying problems facing South East Asian currencies were having a a ripple effect through the region.
"Every currency in the region has been put under the microscope and New Zealand is under a bit of pressure at the moment," he said.
